Content:
In this lesson, we will prove some distributive properties of the Cartesian product.

Content:
The Cartesian product distributes over unions and intersections in much the same way that unions distribute over intersections and vice versa.

Content:
Distributivity over Unions

Content:
The Cartesian product distributes over the union of two sets according to the following laws:

Content:
- [MATH: A \times (B \cup C) = (A \times B) \cup (A \times C)]
- [MATH: (A \cup B) \times C = (A \times C) \cup (B \times C)]

Content:
We can visualize the first rule using the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6adb89f467f79298eb2befc5af5c2886]

Content:
Notice that the rectangle corresponding to the Cartesian product [MATH: A \times (B \cup C)] equals the union of the rectangles corresponding to [MATH: \color{SandyBrown}A \times B] and [MATH: \color{Plum}A \times C.]

Content:
Distributivity over Intersections

Content:
The Cartesian product distributes over the intersection of two sets according to the following laws:

Content:
- [MATH: A \times (B \cap C) = (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)]
- [MATH: (A \cap B) \times C = (A \times C) \cap (B \times C)]

Content:
Again, we can visualize the first rule using the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a4d53a6a0a8d107551c8cac912ab1efe]

Content:
Notice that the rectangle corresponding to the Cartesian product [MATH: A \times (B \cap C)] equals the intersection of the rectangles corresponding to [MATH: \color{SandyBrown}A \times B] and [MATH: \color{Plum}A \times C.]

Content:
Distributivity over Differences

Content:
The Cartesian product distributes over the difference between two sets according to the following laws:

Content:
- [MATH: A \times (B \setminus C) = (A \times B) \setminus (A \times C)]

[MATH: X \subseteq Y \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad \forall x\in U,\: x\in X \Rightarrow x\in Y]

So, to show that [MATH: (A \times B) \cap (C \times D)] is a subset of [MATH: (A\cap C) \times (B\cap D),] we need to demonstrate that a fixed but arbitrary element of the first set is also an element of the second set.

We start by considering an arbitrary element of [MATH: (A \times B) \cap (C \times D)] and use the definition of intersection.

Suppose [MATH: (x, y) \in (A \times B) \cap (C \times D).] Then, by the definition of intersection, we have [MATH: (x,y) \in A \times B] and [MATH: (x,y) \in C \times D.]

Now, let's unfold the second statement using the definition of the Cartesian product.

By the definition of the Cartesian product, since [MATH: (x,y) \in A \times B,] it follows that [MATH: x \in A] and [MATH: y \in B.] Similarly, since [MATH: (x,y) \in C \times D,] it follows that [MATH: x \in C] and [MATH: y \in D.]

Next, we combine the results about [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] separately and use the definition of intersection.

According to the definition of intersection, since [MATH: x \in A] and [MATH: x \in C,] we have [MATH: x \in A \cap C.] Similarly, since [MATH: y \in B] and [MATH: y \in D,] we have [MATH: y \in B \cap D.]

Finally, we use the definition of the Cartesian product again.

Since [MATH: x \in A \cap C] and [MATH: y \in B \cap D,] using the definition of the Cartesian product, we get [MATH: (x,y) \in (A \cap C) \times (B \cap D).]

And we draw our conclusion using the definition of a subset.

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: (A \times B) \cap (C \times D) \subseteq (A\cap C) \times (B\cap D).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will prove some distributive properties of the Cartesian product.

Content:
The Cartesian product distributes over unions and intersections in much the same way that unions distribute over intersections and vice versa.

Content:
Distributivity over Unions

Content:
The Cartesian product distributes over the union of two sets according to the following laws:

Content:
- [MATH: A \times (B \cup C) = (A \times B) \cup (A \times C)]

Content:
Distributivity over Intersections

Content:
The Cartesian product distributes over the intersection of two sets according to the following laws:

Content:
- [MATH: A \times (B \cap C) = (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)]

Distributivity over Differences

Content:
The Cartesian product distributes over the difference between two sets according to the following laws:

- [MATH: A \times (B \setminus C) = (A \times B) \setminus (A \times C)]
